propositions.text: Applicant is Nigerian citizen who arrived in Canada in 2008 as an international student and graduated in 2012 with a BSc in Biological Sciences.
propositions.quote: Ms. Chika Kelechi Osahor [the Applicant] is a citizen of Nigeria. She arrived in Canada in January 2008 as an International Student and studied at the University of Alberta. She graduated in April 2012, with a Bachelor of Science in Biological Sciences.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant is a Nigerian citizen who arrived in Canada in 2008 and graduated in 2012 with a BSc in Biological Sciences.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for a Post Graduate Work Permit and admission to Trent University's Nursing Program, received admission and PGWP valid until 2015.
propositions.quote: Prior to her graduation Ms. Osahor applied for a Post Graduate Work Permit [PGWP] and also applied for admission to the Nursing Program offered at Trent University in Ontario. She did not anticipate admission to Trent, but in June 2012 she received an offer of admission. At the end of June 2012 she was also granted her PWGP, valid until June 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant applied for a PGWP and nursing admission, received both in June 2012, with PGWP valid until 2015.

propositions.text: Applicant contacted Respondent by phone, was advised PGWP could not be cancelled but to apply for new study and off-campus work permits, and could apply for second PGWP after nursing program without using first PGWP.
propositions.quote: On receipt of the PGWP, Ms. Osahor noted that the terms of the work permit included a prohibition against returning to school unless authorized. She reports that she contacted the Respondent by phone, explained her circumstances and was advised that the PGWP could not be cancelled but that she should apply for a new study permit and an off campus work permit. She further reports she was advised that upon completion of the Nursing Program at Trent she would be in a position to apply for a second PGWP so long as she did not use the PWGP issued in June 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant says she was advised by phone that her PGWP could not be cancelled but she should apply for new permits and could apply for a second PGWP after nursing program.

propositions.text: Applicant received renewed study and off-campus work permits, graduated nursing in 2016, applied for second PGWP without disclosing 2012 phone advice to Officer.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osahor received the renewed study permit and an off campus work permit. She graduated from the Trent Nursing Program in January 2016 and was subsequently authorized to practice as a Registered Nurse in Ontario. Not having made use of the initial PGWP, she applied for a second PGWP. In applying for the second PGWP Ms. Osahor’s counsel at the time acknowledged to the Officer that she was seeking a second PGWP, noted she had not worked under the first PGWP and submitted that the Officer considering the application could, in the circumstances, grant a second PGWP. It does not appear that Ms. Osahor’s 2012 telephone conversation with the Respondent or the advice she reports she was given in the course of that conversation was disclosed to the Officer.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant got new permits, graduated nursing, applied for second PGWP, but did not disclose 2012 phone advice to the Officer.

propositions.text: Respondent’s PGWP Program Delivery Instructions provide students are ineligible for a PGWP if one was previously issued; Officer applied this criterion to deny application.
propositions.quote: The Respondent’s PGWP Program Delivery Instructions [PDI] provide that students are not eligible to be issued a PGWP if a PWGP has been previously issued. In denying Ms. Osahor’s application the Officer applied this criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker applied the PGWP Program Delivery Instructions denying second PGWP if one was previously issued, and denied the applicant's application accordingly.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Officer fettered discretion by applying PGWP-PDI as law and failed to consider unique circumstances; alleges breach of legitimate expectation from 2012 phone advice.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osahor submits that in refusing her application the Officer applied the PGWP-PDI as if they were law, that the Officer failed to consider her unique circumstances, and that this in turn amounted to a fettering of discretion. She further submits that there was a breach of the doctrine of legitimate expectation based on the information provided over the phone by the Respondent in 2012.

propositions.text: Respondent argues PGWP-PDI are mandatory and legitimate expectation cannot extend substantive rights to applicant.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the PGWP-PDI are mandatory in this respect and that the doctrine of legitimate expectation cannot be relied upon to extend substantive rights to Ms. Osahor.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the Officer fettered discretion and breached legitimate expectation; the Respondent says PGWP-PDI are mandatory and legitimate expectation cannot extend rights.

propositions.text: The application turns on whether the Officer unreasonably applied PGWP-PDI restrictions to deny a second PGWP.
propositions.quote: Having considered the Parties’ submissions, I am of the opinion that the Application turns on a single issue, whether the Officer unreasonably interpreted and applied the restrictions within PGWP-PDI in declaring students ineligible to receive a second PGWP.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Officer to apply the criteria and refuse the application; the application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow I am of the opinion that it was reasonable for the Officer to conclude the criteria were to be applied and the refusal of the Application on the facts disclosed was also reasonable. The Application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the issue is whether the Officer unreasonably applied PGWP-PDI; concludes the Officer acted reasonably and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: Applicant submits fettering of discretion and procedural fairness issues are reviewed on correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osahor submits that the issues pertaining to fettering of discretion and procedural fairness are to be reviewed against the standard of correctness.

propositions.text: Respondent submits findings of fact and mixed fact-law are reviewed on reasonableness; procedural fairness on correctness.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that findings of fact and of mixed fact and law are to be reviewed against a standard of reasonableness whereas questions of procedural fairness and natural justice are reviewable on a correctness standard.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues fettering and procedural fairness issues require correctness review; the Respondent says fact findings are reasonableness, procedural fairness correctness.

propositions.text: Deference is normally given to decision-maker’s interpretation of their home statute; court intervenes only if decision is unjustified, unintelligible, or unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Deference will normally be extended to a decision-maker’s interpretation and application of their home statute (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 54, [2008] 1 SCR 190 [Dunsmuir]). A reviewing court will not normally intervene where the decision-making process is justified, transparent and intelligible, and the decision is within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes defensible in respect of the facts and law (Dunsmuir, at para 47).

propositions.text: Core issue relates to interpretation and application of PGWP-PDI within IRPA framework.
propositions.quote: The core issue raised by Ms. Osahor relates to the interpretation and application of the PGWP-PDI within the legislative and regulatory framework established by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: The court states deference is given to decision-maker’s interpretation of their statute; the core issue is interpretation of PGWP-PDI within IRPA.

propositions.text: Prior jurisprudence on standard of review may be adopted; Nookala applied reasonableness standard to PGWP-PDI interpretation.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, where prior jurisprudence has determined the standard of review to be applied in considering a particular issue a reviewing court may adopt that standard (Dunsmuir, at para 62). In Nookala v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1019, 46 Imm LR (4th) 287, Justice Anne Mactavish addressed a question similar to that raised here, whether an applicant must satisfy the PGWP-PDI criteria. In addressing the issue Justice Mactavish adopted a reasonableness standard of review (Nookala, at para 10, see also Abubacker v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 1112 at paras 14 and 17, [2016] FCJ No 1111 (QL) [Abubacker] and Rehman v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1021 at para 7, [2015] FCJ No 1015 (QL) [Rehman]).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes prior cases adopted reasonableness standard for PGWP-PDI interpretation, including Nookala, Abubacker, and Rehman.

propositions.text: Interpretation of IRPA scheme is reviewed on reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: As noted above the core issue relates to the interpretation of the IRPA scheme, a matter that the jurisprudence establishes is to be reviewed against a reasonableness standard.

paragraphs.summary: The court states interpretation of the IRPA scheme is reviewed on a reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Applicant argues PGWP program is policy, PGWP-PDI are guidelines, officers have discretion to issue second PGWP in special circumstances; officer erred by strict application here.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osahor submits that the law does not prevent the issuance of a second or replacement PGWP. She argues that the PGWP program is a product of policy and the PGWP-PDI are a policy document that is to be interpreted and applied by decision-makers as a guideline. In effect, she submits that an officer considering applications pursuant to the PGWP-PDI is not prevented by law from issuing a second PGWP where special circumstances exist. She submits that in failing to recognize this discretion, and by abiding strictly to the PGWP-PDI requirements without consideration of her particular circumstances the Officer in this case erred. She further argues that the special circumstances evidenced in this case warranted the exercise of discretion and the granting of a second PGWP. I disagree.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with applicant’s argument that officers have discretion to waive PGWP-PDI criteria and grant second PGWP in special circumstances.
propositions.quote: She submits that in failing to recognize this discretion, and by abiding strictly to the PGWP-PDI requirements without consideration of her particular circumstances the Officer in this case erred. She further argues that the special circumstances evidenced in this case warranted the exercise of discretion and the granting of a second PGWP. I disagree.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues PGWP-PDI are guidelines allowing discretion to grant second PGWP; the court disagrees and finds no such discretion.

propositions.text: Parties agree PGWP is not in IRPA or IRPR but authorized under section 205 of IRPR, which allows Minister to designate work and criteria for limited labour market access.
propositions.quote: The Parties agree that the PGWP is not expressly provided for in the IRPA or the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [IRPR], but rather is made available to applicants pursuant to the authority provided the Minister under section 205 of the IRPR. Section 205 states in part: 205 A work permit may be issued under section 200 to a foreign national who intends to perform work that […] (c) is designated by the Minister as being work that can be performed by a foreign national on the basis of the following criteria, namely, […] (ii) limited access to the Canadian labour market is necessary for reasons of public policy relating to the competitiveness of Canada’s academic institutions or economy; or 205 Un permis de travail peut être délivré à l’étranger en vertu de l’article 200 si le travail pour lequel le permis est demandé satisfait à l’une ou l’autre des conditions suivantes : […] c) il est désigné par le ministre comme travail pouvant être exercé par des étrangers, sur la base des critères suivants : […] (ii) un accès limité au marché du travail au Canada est justifiable pour des raisons d’intérêt public en rapport avec la compétitivité des établissements universitaires ou de l’économie du Canada;

paragraphs.summary: The court states parties agree PGWP is authorized under IRPR section 205, allowing Minister to designate work and criteria for limited labour market access.

propositions.text: Section 205 authorizes Minister to set program criteria for limited labour market access; Minister must establish criteria for PGWP.
propositions.quote: In effect, section 205 of the IRPR extends to the Minister the authority to provide foreign nationals with limited access to the Canadian labour market where that access satisfies public policy objectives relating to the competiveness of Canada’s economy or academic institutions. The IRPR do not prescribe criteria but rather authorize the Minister to both designate the work to be performed and define how, or on what basis, limited access is to be provided. In doing so the Minister must be in a position to establish program criteria.

propositions.text: Justice Mactavish in Nookala held PGWP Program document establishes mandatory criteria and officers have no discretion to waive eligibility requirements.
propositions.quote: As noted by Justice Mactavish at paragraphs 11 and 12 of Nookala: [11] Fettering of discretion occurs when a decision-maker treats guidelines as mandatory: see, for example, Canadian Reformed Church of Cloverdale B.C. v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Social Development), 2015 FC 1075, 2015 F.C.J. No. 1089. The operative portion of the document establishing the Post‑Graduation Work Permit Program is not, however, a “guideline”, as that term is used in the jurisprudence: see, for example, Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at para. 32, 3 S.C.R. 909. [12] The Program document at issue in this case establishes criteria that must be satisfied for a candidate to qualify for a Post‑Graduation Work Permit. While the Program document also provides information and guidance as to how the program is to be administered, nothing in the document confers any discretion on immigration officers to modify or waive the Program’s eligibility requirements. Consequently, no fettering of discretion occurred when the immigration officer determined that Mr. Nookala was required to hold a valid study permit in order for him to be eligible for a Post‑Graduation Work Permit. [Emphasis added]

paragraphs.summary: The court explains section 205 authorizes Minister to set PGWP criteria; Nookala held PGWP criteria are mandatory and officers have no discretion to waive them.

propositions.text: PGWP-PDI provide criteria and guidance; applicant argues Nookala and similar cases can be distinguished as obiter because they rely on IRPR section 199, but court is unconvinced.
propositions.quote: As Justice Mactavish notes in Nookala, the PGWP- PDI is a document that provides information, guidance, and sets out program criteria. Ms. Osahor argues that Nookala, as well as the decisions of this Court in Abubaker and Rehman where Justices Sandra Simpson and Denis Gascon reached conclusions that accord with those of Justice Mactavish, can be distinguished from the case at hand. She submits that in each of these cases the PGWP-PDI requirements in issue found their basis in section 199 of the IRPR, a section that identifies criteria a foreign national must satisfy in applying for a work permit from within Canada. In effect Ms. Osahor argues that the finding in these cases is to the effect that the mandatory program criteria as established in the PGWP-PDI is obiter. I am unconvinced.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds PGWP-PDI set criteria; applicant argues prior cases relying on IRPR section 199 are obiter, but court is unconvinced.

propositions.text: Prior cases reviewed on reasonableness standard found PGWP-PDI criteria mandatory; this applies here.
propositions.quote: In each of the above noted cases the decisions before the Court were reviewed on a standard of reasonableness and the issue was whether it was reasonable for the decision-maker to apply the criteria set out in the PGWP-PDI. In Nookala, Justice Mactavish makes no reference to IRPR section 199 but does conclude “[t]he program document at issue in this case establishes criteria that must be satisfied for a candidate to qualify for a Post-graduate Work Permit [Emphasis Added]” (Nookala, at para 12). This conclusion was also adopted in Abubaker at paragraph 16. In Rehman, Justice Gascon does address section 199 but then proceeded to note that the PGWP-PDI establish “distinct requirements” that an applicant must meet (Rehman, at para 19). This is exactly the circumstance before the Court in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds prior cases applying reasonableness review held PGWP-PDI criteria mandatory, as here.

propositions.text: Minister authorized under IRPR section 205 to set PGWP criteria; Officer reasonably applied criteria and no procedural fairness breach found.
propositions.quote: The Minister is granted the authority pursuant to section 205 of the IRPR to set out criteria for the issuance of a PGWP. Having established those criteria in the PGWP-PDI it was reasonable for the Officer considering Ms. Osahor’s application to conclude that those specific requirements could not be ignored. I am also unable to find any breach of procedural fairness arising out of the doctrine of legitimate expectations.

propositions.text: Officer was not advised of 2012 phone conversation; applicant cannot now argue Officer erred in failing to consider it.
propositions.quote: The Officer was not advised of the content of the 2012 telephone conversation on which Ms. Osahor now relies. Not having provided notice of this conversation to the Officer, it is not now open to Ms. Osahor to argue on judicial review that the Officer erred in failing to consider and address those circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer reasonably applied criteria and no procedural fairness breach; applicant did not disclose 2012 phone advice to Officer.

propositions.text: Applicant requests certification of question whether applying PGWP-PDI as mandatory fetters Visa Officer’s discretion.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osahor’s counsel has proposed the following question for certification: In applying the criteria found in the Program Delivery Instructions for the Post-Graduation work permit program as mandatory and akin to statutory rules or delegated legislation, is a Visa Officer fettering his or her discretion?

paragraphs.summary: The applicant requests certification of a question whether applying PGWP-PDI as mandatory fetters Visa Officer discretion.

propositions.text: To certify a question it must be dispositive and of general importance beyond parties’ interests (Zhang).
propositions.quote: To be certified, a question must be dispositive of the appeal and raise a question of general importance that transcends the interests of the parties (Zhang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FCA 168 at para 9, [2014] 4 FCR 290).

paragraphs.summary: The court states certification requires a dispositive question of general importance per Zhang.

propositions.text: Zhang criteria for certification not met here.
propositions.quote: In my opinion the Zhang criteria have not been satisfied here.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the certification criteria under Zhang are not met here.

propositions.text: The PGWP-PDI set out qualifying criteria characterized as mandatory in this court's jurisprudence, a position adopted here.
propositions.quote: The PGWP-PDI do set out qualifying criteria and those criteria have been characterized as criteria that must be satisfied in the jurisprudence of this court, a position that I have adopted within the context of this particular case.

propositions.text: The dispositive issue is the reasonableness of the Officer’s decision to follow the criteria, not whether the criteria are mandatory.
propositions.quote: However, the dispositive issue in this case was the reasonableness of the Officer’s determination to follow the criteria, and not that the criteria were adopted or treated as mandatory in nature.

paragraphs.summary: The court states PGWP-PDI criteria are characterized as mandatory but the key issue is the reasonableness of the Officer's decision to follow them.

propositions.text: If the distinction about mandatory nature is wrong, the second Zhang criterion prevents certification as it is not satisfied.
propositions.quote: However, if I am wrong in drawing a distinction between whether the PWGP-PDI criteria are mandatory in nature and the overall reasonableness of the Officer’s decision to follow them, the second of the Zhang criteria also prevents certification as it has not been satisfied.

propositions.text: The issue has been considered by this Court three times; jurisprudence is not split or inconsistent on it.
propositions.quote: The issue raised in this Application has been previously considered by this Court on three separate occasions. The Court’s jurisprudence is not split or inconsistent on the issue.

propositions.text: Where jurisprudence has sufficiently answered a question, an issue of general importance does not arise (citing Lai and NK cases).
propositions.quote: Where the jurisprudence has sufficiently answered a question an issue of general importance does not arise (Lai v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2015 FCA 21, at paras 4-10, 29 Imm LR (4th) 211; NK v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2015 FC 1377 at paras 62, 80, 102, [2015] F.C.J. No. 1449 (QL)).

paragraphs.summary: The court says if the mandatory distinction is wrong, certification fails under Zhang; the issue is settled by prior jurisprudence, citing Lai and NK.

propositions.text: The request to certify the question is denied and the Application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The request to certify the above question is denied and the Application is dismissed.

propositions.text: This Court's judgment is that the Application is dismissed and no question is certified.
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the Application is dismissed. No question is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court denies certification and dismisses the Application, giving its judgment accordingly.
